article_title: QuestDB 10.0 Ships QWP, a Binary Protocol Unifying Writes and Arrow Reads Over a Single Connection
summary: Approved. The sole automated finding was a source-allowlist config gap for QuestDB's own official blog, not a content or attribution issue; every claim, quote, and figure in the article was independently verified verbatim against the two source snapshots, and the allowlist gap has been fixed at the root.

content_preview.title: QuestDB 10.0 Ships QWP, a Binary Protocol Unifying Writes and Arrow Reads Over a Single Connection
content_preview.summary: QuestDB 10.0 introduces QWP, a binary columnar protocol that replaces separate ILP and PostgreSQL wire connections, cutting ingestion overhead and streaming query results into Apache Arrow at over 200 million rows a second.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

QuestDB released version 10.0.0 of its open-source time-series database on August 6, 2026, headlined by a new wire protocol that lets a single client connection handle both writes and query results, according to the [release notes on GitHub](https://github.com/questdb/questdb/releases/tag/10.0.0). editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News piece (Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know / Analysis) at 1,123 words, within the 400-1200 word range for the News category. Quantitative claims are consistently attributed ('according to the release notes', 'the company reports', 'QuestDB says') rather than stated as bare fact, and the piece proactively separates the open-source 10.0 release from the paid Enterprise 4.0 announcement in the same blog post so readers do not conflate the two.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read both source snapshots from disk at sources/2026-08/questdb-100-ships-qwp-a-binary-protocol-unifying-writes-and-arrow-reads-over-a-single-connection/ (source-0.html.gz = GitHub release notes, source-1.html.gz = QuestDB blog post). Re-decompressed and re-hashed both; sha256 matched manifest.json exactly for each (37c9fbd0...16e0a777 and abe22be0...9d80667b9), confirming no drift between what chief:review fetched and what was reviewed. Both returned HTTP 200, no archive_fallback, no suspicious_patterns entries in the manifest for either source. Extracted full plain text from both and checked every specific claim, number, and quotation in article.body_markdown against it: the 'in excess of 200M rows/second, with first-batch latency of a handful of milliseconds' quote (verbatim in source-0); the '3-4x less space' compression quote (verbatim in source-0); the full client-support table (Java/C++/Rust/Python full, Go/.NET beta, Node.js 'Coming in a later release' — verbatim in source-0); all three breaking changes cited (SHOW PARTITIONS trailing columns, EXPLAIN plain-text output, SecurityContext's two new authorization methods — all verbatim/accurate summaries of source-0's Breaking Changes section); the ClickBench sorting figure (52ms -> 37ms, verbatim in source-0); kurtosis()/skewness() and scalar sub-query additions (verbatim in source-0). From source-1 (blog): the 3.6x-over-network / 3.1x-single-machine ingestion figures and the underlying 347-byte vs 97-byte TSBS row sizes on a 14.7 Gbit/s link (verbatim); the 220-million-rows/second Arrow egress figure, the 500M-row/2.3s drain, 32ms first-Arrow-batch figure, and the 1.55x/2.35x ClickHouse comparisons (verbatim, matching the chart figures in the post); the 18.8 vs 21.4/27.0/64.3 bytes-per-row figures (verbatim); the 'Fast ingestion is what QuestDB is known for...' and 'ILP and the PostgreSQL wire protocol are both still here...' and 'so it never gets your database credentials' quotes (all verbatim); the MCP client list (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor — verbatim); the covering-index 9.4.0 origin and the 20M-row/8-worker/10%-selectivity benchmark table showing 3.0x-3.8x speedups (verbatim, matches article's stated range exactly); and the Enterprise 4.0 'ships in the next few days' framing as a distinct commercial product (verbatim, and the article correctly flags this in 'What We Don't Know' as separate from the OSS 10.0 release under review). No hallucinated quotes, no misattributed specifics, no orphan URLs — every body-cited URL also appears in article.sources. No suspicious_patterns to evaluate (both manifest entries were null).
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every number, quote, and specific in the article traces directly to one of the two cited sources and was independently confirmed against the raw snapshot text rather than against the article's own paraphrase of it. Zero fabricated or misattributed specifics found across an unusually dense, benchmark-heavy article.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and consistently hedged. The 'What We Don't Know' section is doing real editorial work here, not boilerplate: it explicitly notes that QuestDB's own account says fuller third-party-replicable methodology posts are still pending ('the egress one follows shortly'), meaning the 3.6x and 220M-rows figures currently rest on the company's own numbers only, and it separates the unrelated paid Enterprise 4.0 announcement from the OSS release being covered. The Analysis section is clearly-labeled editorial interpretation, not a sourced claim.
editor_notes.originality: Searched src/content/articles/ for any prior QuestDB or QWP coverage (grep -ril questdb) — none found. No other time-series-database release covered in the last several weeks of src/content/articles/2026-08/. Genuinely new topic, not a duplicate or rewrite of existing coverage.
concerns: The automated script flagged questdb.com as 'not in allowlist'. On inspection this is a config gap, not a source-quality problem: questdb.com is QuestDB's own official site/blog, the primary first-party source for its own open-source project's release announcements, directly parallel to already-allowlisted open-source-project domains in the same 'Cloud, devops, and developer tools / official project sites' section (postgresql.org, valkey.io, blog.jetbrains.com, blog.rust-lang.org). This mirrors the precedent set in the 2026-07-18 Samsung Flex Titanium review, where an analogous allowlist gap for a company's own official domain was fixed at the root rather than filed as a reader-facing correction, since filing a correction for a non-error would misleadingly imply a factual problem exists. Fixed at the root: added questdb.com to config/source_allowlist.txt under the existing 'Cloud, devops, and developer tools / official project sites' section.

Both cited sources (GitHub release notes and QuestDB's own blog) are affiliated with QuestDB itself, with no independent third-party corroboration of the headline performance figures (200M+/220M rows/sec, 3.6x ingestion speedup, ClickHouse/TimescaleDB comparisons). This is a real limitation, but it is standard and previously-accepted practice on this outlet for product/release-announcement News pieces — see the Samsung Flex Titanium piece (Samsung's own press site + newsroom only), the Arista 7060XE7 piece (Arista's own press release as sole source), the Masdar financing piece (masdar.ae as sole source, both citations), and the JFrog PixelSmash disclosure (jfrog.com blog as sole source), all of which were approved (with or without unrelated corrections) on a single-vendor sourcing profile. The article itself flags the lack of independent replication explicitly in 'What We Don't Know', which is the correct editorial mitigation for this profile rather than a reason to withhold publication.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: High-quality, meticulously sourced News submission — every one of an unusually large number of specific figures and quotes was independently verified verbatim against the two disk snapshots, with zero discrepancies found. The only automated finding was a source-allowlist configuration gap for QuestDB's own legitimate official domain, which parallels prior-accepted single-vendor sourcing for release-announcement News pieces on this outlet and has been corrected at the root in config/source_allowlist.txt rather than filed as a misleading reader-facing correction. Verdict overridden from the script's suggested APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS to APPROVE on that basis.
